stem: A 32-year-old patient presents with small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques on the elbows and knees, involving less than 5% of the body surface area. The patient reports mild itching but is otherwise healthy. Considering the extent and severity of the disease, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
keywords: “<5% body surface area” – Indicates limited/mild psoriasis, pointing to topical therapy.
“Small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques” – Classic description of plaque psoriasis, confirming the type of lesion.
“Mild itching, otherwise healthy” – Suggests mild disease with no systemic involvement, ruling out systemic therapy.

D.title: Topical corticosteroids
D.body:
Topical corticosteroids are first-line therapy for limited plaque psoriasis (<5% body surface area).
They reduce inflammation, erythema, and scaling by inhibiting keratinocyte proliferation, and suppressing local immune responses in the skin.
Potency is selected based on lesion location (low-medium potency for face/flexures, high potency for elbows/knees).
Safe for short-term and intermittent use, and effective in mild, localized disease.

A.title: Systemic corticosteroids
A.body:
Not recommended for psoriasis due to risk of rebound flares and pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.
Reserved only for severe, refractory cases or specific complications.

B.title: PUVA (Psoralen + UVA therapy)
B.body:
Used in moderate to severe or extensive psoriasis, not for limited disease.
Requires multiple sessions and monitoring for skin cancer risk and phototoxicity.

C.title: Biologics
C.body:
Reserved for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis or cases unresponsive to topical/systemic therapy.
High cost and potential immunosuppression; overkill for <5% BSA involvement.

E.title: Methotrexate
E.body:
Systemic therapy for severe, extensive, or rapidly progressing psoriasis.
Requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression, so not suitable for mild, localized disease.

keyConcept:
Mild, limited plaque psoriasis (<5% BSA) is treated first-line with topical corticosteroids.
Systemic therapies (methotrexate, biologics, systemic corticosteroids, PUVA) are reserved for moderate to severe or refractory disease.

featureTableName: Plaque Psoriasis: Mild / Limited Disease Management
differentialDiagnosisTableName: Dermatology – Plaque Psoriasis – Mild / Limited Disease Management Differential Diagnosis of Mild / Limited Plaque Psoriasis

featureTable.description: Plaque psoriasis involving <5% body surface area
Small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques; mild itching
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Common sites: extensor surfaces; no systemic involvement
Low-to-medium potency for face/flexures; high potency for elbows/knees

featureTable.description: Vitamin D analogs (calcipotriol), coal tar, moisturizers
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Can be combined with corticosteroids for synergistic effect

featureTable.description: Reserved for moderate to severe psoriasis
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Methotrexate, biologics, PUVA; not indicated for <5% BSA

featureTable.description: Assess response in 2–4 weeks; monitor for side effects
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Educate patient on intermittent use and adherence

differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Typically ill-defined borders, more flexural involvement, acute flares

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Annular, scaly plaques with central clearing
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Positive KOH mount; often single or few lesions; responds to antifungals
Violaceous color, Wickham striae; usually pruritic; mucosal involvement possible

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Greasy, yellowish scales on scalp, face, chest
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Distribution favors seborrheic areas; less sharply demarcated

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Herald patch followed by Christmas-tree pattern
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Self-limiting; characteristic eruption pattern; usually trunk involvement

diagram.name: Plaque Psoriasis: Mild / Limited Disease Management
diagram.caption: The diagram illustrates mild plaque psoriasis (<5% BSA) with small, well-demarcated scaly plaques on elbows and knees, highlighting first-line treatment with topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs, and moisturizers. It also shows follow-up recommendations and indicates advanced therapies (methotrexate, biologics, PUVA) reserved for moderate to severe or uncontrolled disease (>10% BSA).
